title: Ensuring Government's Shared Responsibility Framework for Equitable Sharing of Losses in Bank Scams Offers Adequate Protection
what_it_is: Ensuring Government's Shared Responsibility Framework for Equitable Sharing of Losses in Bank Scams Offers Adequate Protection

sections.label: Anti-scam duties and payouts
sections.summary: The SRF sets anti-scam duties for financial institutions and telcos and provides payouts to phishing scam victims when duties are breached.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
sentences.text: The SRF prescribes a set of anti-scam duties for financial institutions (FIs) and telecommunication companies (telcos) and provides for payouts to victims of phishing scams when these duties are breached.

sections.label: Phishing scam cases and losses
sections.summary: MAS estimates about 15,000 phishing scam cases from 2021 to mid-2023, with an average loss of about S$3,900 per case.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
sentences.text: Based on data collected by the Police, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) estimates there were about 15,000 phishing scam cases from 2021 to mid-2023, with an average loss per case of about S$3,900.

sections.label: Phishing scam numbers and proportion
sections.summary: Phishing scams rose in the first half of this year but fell as a proportion of total scam cases from 17% to 13%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
sentences.text: As it stands today, the number of phishing scams has continued to rise in the first half of this year compared to the previous period, but has declined as a proportion of total scam cases from 17% to 13%.

sections.label: Waterfall approach versus UK compensation
sections.summary: MAS acknowledges the waterfall approach differs drastically from the UK, where banks must compensate customers unless fraudulent or grossly negligent.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The waterfall approach that is described in the paper, of course, MAS acknowledges that it is actually quite drastically different from the approach being taken in the United Kingdom (UK), where there is going to be a default requirement for banks to compensate customers, unless the customer was fraudulent or grossly negligent.

sections.label: Bank duties and physical tokens
sections.summary: A Member asks how different the approach is from banks' current duties and whether victims will remain uncompensated, and says banks phased out physical tokens.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I do not know whether fully or progressively.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: So, how different is it really from the current status of the banks fulfilling these duties, and is the Government concerned that many scam victims will remain uncompensated under the SRF framework?

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: He mentioned that customers can request for physical tokens from the banks.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I have received many emails from the public to say that this is not offered by their banks, they were told that it has been phased out.

sections.label: App restrictions and money lock
sections.summary: Access to apps is restricted when risky apps are detected, and DBS, OCBC and UOB will implement money lock this month.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
sentences.text: These restrict customers' access to their apps, if potentially malicious risky apps not uploaded from official stores or portals, are detected on the customers phones.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
sentences.text: I wanted to update the Member also on how banks are exploring "money lock", which allows customers to set aside an amount in their bank accounts which cannot be digitally transferred out without strict authentication measures.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
sentences.text: For now, DBS, OCBC and UOB will be implementing their versions of "money lock" this month.

sections.label: SRF feedback and operationalisation
sections.summary: Feedback will be reviewed and the SRF is intended to be operationalised by early next year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
sentences.text: So, we will take all of the feedback, which have been given to us, and we will review that at the end of it.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
sentences.text: We intend to operationalise the SRF by early next year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
sentences.text: These are different duties that either the FIs or telcos have to fulfil.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
sentences.text: So, if there are different scenarios that the SRF would benefit from referencing, I think these will be very helpful, as we roll out and operationalise the SRF.

sections.label: Physical tokens friction with banks
sections.summary: They will work with banks to reduce friction in consumers requesting and receiving physical tokens.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
sentences.text: As I mentioned earlier on, we will work with the banks to ensure that for the physical tokens, there is less friction in consumers requesting for and receiving their physical tokens.

sections.label: Telcos in reimbursement framework
sections.summary: Singapore is the first jurisdiction to include telcos in this reimbursement framework.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
sentences.text: In fact, we are the first jurisdiction in the world to include telcos in this reimbursement framework.

sections.label: Malware scams and SRF review
sections.summary: Malware scams are not yet suited to the framework but will be reviewed in subsequent SRF updates.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
sentences.text: But they are not yet suited to address malware scams because of the evolving and developing nature of malware scams.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
sentences.text: But I want to assure both Members and, in fact, Members of this House, that we will review this new scam variant, such as malware, as part of subsequent updates of SRF.

sections.label: Case-by-case waterfall and goodwill payments
sections.summary: Liability depends case-by-case under the waterfall approach, striking a fair balance; banks have operationalised goodwill payments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
sentences.text: To the second question, it depends on a case-by-case basis.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
sentences.text: So, for now, if it is unauthorised transactions and if it goes through the waterfall approach, for example, if the FIs have fulfilled their duties, the telcos have fulfilled their duties and, in this case, the customers themselves have fulfilled their duties, then it is up to the banks also to see whether they can implement.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
sentences.text: Importantly, it is that, for it to be fair to the FIs, the telcos as well as consumers, we have to strike a fair balance between responsibility of the FIs and telcos as well as consumers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
sentences.text: So, the goodwill payment framework has already been operationalised by the banks.

sections.label: Phishing scam liability under waterfall
sections.summary: For unauthorised phishing transactions, liability under the waterfall framework is borne by the FI if found.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
sentences.text: If it is an unauthorised transaction and it is a phishing scam, then, depending on how the particular case falls under and goes through the waterfall framework, if there is a liability, if it is found that the FI has to bear, they will bear.
